transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s a bit hard to explain, but I’ll try my best because it’s really been bothering me lately, and honestly, it’s been going on for a while, but it’s just gotten so much worse. I came in because I feel like I just cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It’s this awful, constant feeling. Like, I’ll be sitting down in my favorite chair—the one by the window where I usually watch the birds—and I should be relaxing, especially at my age, you know? I’m 66, I’m not working anymore, I should be enjoying my time. But instead, my mind is just racing, and my body feels like it’s humming, like a car engine that’s been left running in the driveway. I feel this overwhelming urge to just jump up and do the next thing, even when I am completely worn out. I’ll be exhausted, my joints will be aching, and I know I should be sitting still, but I just can’t. I’ll get up to organize a drawer that doesn’t need organizing, or I’ll start pacing around the kitchen, wiping down counters that are already clean. It’s like there’s a motor inside me that won’t shut off, and it’s exhausting, it really is. I just want to be able to sit and read a book or watch a television program without feeling like I’m going to jump out of my own skin if I don’t move. It’s just so frustrating, and I don’t know why I can’t just be at peace.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind and feel like you can't stop thinking about them?

Repeating thoughts? Like the exact same thing over and over? No, I wouldn't say that. It’s actually quite the opposite, if I’m being completely honest with you. It’s not one thought stuck on a loop, it’s more like... well, it’s like a television where someone is just flipping the channels constantly and you can't even settle on a picture. My late husband used to do that with the remote control in the evenings, just click, click, click, never staying on one program long enough to know what the story was even about. It used to drive me absolutely up the wall, and now that’s exactly what my own brain is doing to me! 

It's never just one thing that gets stuck. I’ll be thinking about whether I need to buy more milk at the store, and then suddenly I’m thinking about the dust on the baseboards in the hallway, and then I’m wondering about my neighbor's dog that was barking earlier, and then I’m deciding if I should take the living room curtains down and wash them, even though I just washed them in the spring. 

So, no, it’s never just one specific thought that I can’t get rid of or stop thinking about. I almost wish it was just one thought, to be perfectly frank! At least then I could maybe focus on it for a minute and do something about it. But no, I don't get stuck on one specific worry or idea like that. It's just this constant, exhausting stream of a hundred different things flying by all at once, and I can't hold onto any of them.
Do you often feel anxious or fearful about things that are happening or might happen?

Well, anxious or fearful... no, I really wouldn't use those words. It's funny you ask that because my sister, she is an absolute worrier. She watches the evening news and gets herself into a real state about the economy, or the weather, or what might happen to her grandkids, and she will just fret and fret over it. But me? No, I really don't have that kind of fear hanging over my head at all. I am not sitting here biting my nails about what is going to happen tomorrow or next week. 

People always seem to assume that when you can't sit still, you must be nervous about something. My neighbor, Martha, she came over just last Tuesday to drop off some mail that got delivered to her house by mistake. The mail carrier has been doing that a lot lately, just dropping things wherever, which is a whole other frustrating thing, but anyway, she saw me pacing around the living room and asked what had me so anxious. And I had to tell her that I wasn't anxious in the slightest! I was just trying to figure out what to do with myself because I felt like I needed to go out and clean the gutters, even though I have the knees of a 66-year-old woman and shouldn't be anywhere near a ladder. 

So, no, it is not a worry about the future or a fear of things happening. I don't walk around dreading things. I don't lay in bed at night afraid of what might go wrong in the world. I lay in bed at night because my brain is going a mile a minute about a hundred silly little things, like whether I should reorganize the pantry or if I remembered to water the ferns on the porch. But it is never fear. It is just... well, just that busyness I was telling you about.
Are you having trouble sleeping at night?

Trouble sleeping? Well, yes and no, I suppose. It’s not that I can’t sleep once I finally drift off—once I’m out, I’m usually out until the morning, unless the neighbor’s dog starts up again or the garbage truck comes clattering down the street earlier than usual. They’ve been coming at 5:30 in the morning lately, can you believe that? Who needs their trash picked up before the sun is even shining? 

But getting to sleep, oh, that is a whole different story entirely. That’s where the real trouble is. I’ll do my whole routine, you know? I’ll wash my face, brush my teeth, put on my favorite blue flannel nightgown—the one my daughter bought me for Christmas two years ago, it’s so soft—and I’ll get into bed. I’ll turn out the lamp, and I’ll tell myself, "Alright, time to rest." And my body is tired, doctor. Like I said, my joints ache, my back gets stiff, I am physically ready to sleep. 

But my brain? My brain decides that the moment my head hits the pillow is the perfect time to start running through that endless list of things I was telling you about. I’ll lay there staring at the ceiling, and suddenly I’m thinking about the living room curtains again. And then I’m wondering if I should call my sister tomorrow, even though she’ll just talk my ear off about the stock market. And then I’m thinking about how I need to sort through the old photo albums in the hall closet. It’s just flip, flip, flip, channel surfing in my head. I’ll toss and turn, and I’ll try to get comfortable, but I just feel so restless. Sometimes I even have to get up and walk around the house for a bit, maybe go into the kitchen and wipe down the counter one more time, just to burn off some of that... that energy, I guess you’d call it. It can take me hours to finally quiet down enough to actually fall asleep. So, yes, the nights can be very, very long and frustrating, but it’s not because I’m worried or afraid, it’s just because my mind won’t turn off the lights when the rest of me is ready to go to bed.
Are you finding it difficult to complete your daily tasks because of these feelings and thoughts?

Well, completing daily tasks... yes, yes, I suppose that is exactly what's happening, and it is just so frustrating. It's not that I don't want to do things, you see. I have always been a doer. But lately, it's like I just can't seem to get from the beginning of a task all the way to the end without getting completely derailed. 

Take my quilting charity, for example. I've been volunteering with them for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We make these beautiful lap quilts for the veterans' hospital over in the next county. Anyway, the coordinator, Susan—she's a lovely woman, but very organized, very particular about how things are done—she'll give me a list of three or four things to do. She'll say, "Okay, I need you to sort these fabric squares by color, then press the backing material, and then box up the finished quilts for transport." 

And I have every intention of doing exactly what she asks! I'll dive right in, I'll grab those fabric squares and start making my little piles—blues here, reds there, the floral patterns in a separate stack. I'll start the first task right away with all the energy in the world. But then... well, then I'll realize the ironing board needs to be set up for the backing material, so I'll go to the closet to get it. But while I'm in the closet, I'll notice that the donation bins are overflowing and need to be reorganized, so I'll start pulling those out. And then I'll find a stray spool of thread on the floor, and I'll walk over to the sewing machine to put it away, and while I'm there, I'll decide to oil the machine because it was squeaking last week... 

And before I know it, an hour has gone by, I'm covered in dust from the closet, my hands are oily, the fabric squares are only half sorted, the ironing board is still put away, and those finished quilts certainly haven't been boxed up. I just wander right into another chore, and then another, and the last steps of what I was actually supposed to be doing just never get done. It's like I leave a trail of half-finished projects behind me everywhere I go, and it drives me absolutely crazy because I know Susan is relying on me, but I just get so sidetracked by every little thing that catches my eye!
Do you often find yourself doing things on impulse, without fully thinking them through?

On impulse? Without thinking? Oh, goodness, no, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, it’s almost the exact opposite, if you really want to know. I don’t just jump into things blindly. You want to talk about impulsive, you should meet my sister-in-law, Carol. Now, Carol, she will just go out on a Tuesday afternoon to buy a gallon of milk and come home with a brand new dining room set. Just like that! Swipes the credit card, doesn't even measure the room to see if the table will fit. And of course, it didn't fit, they had to take the leaf out and push it right up against the radiator, which is a terrible fire hazard if you ask me, but that's Carol for you. 

But me? No, I don't do things like that. I don't make snap decisions or do things without thinking them through. If anything, I think about them too much! Like I was saying before with the quilting, or the chores around the house... I have a plan. I really do. I think about exactly what needs to be done. I’ll say to myself, "Okay, today we are going to deep clean the guest bathroom because the grout is looking a little dingy." I think it all through. It’s just that... well, the plan gets a little scrambled once I actually start moving. I might end up in the garage organizing the gardening tools instead of scrubbing the grout, but it’s not because I just impulsively decided to build a garden out of nowhere! It’s just that one thought leads to another, and then another, and my body just sort of follows along. 

So, no, I don't do things on a whim or act reckless. I don't make wild purchases or anything of that sort. I'm actually very sensible about my decisions. Living on a fixed income and all, you really have to be. You can't just go around acting on impulse when you're 66 years old and relying on a pension and Social Security, you know? The price of eggs alone these days is enough to make you think twice before you even drive down to the grocery store! So, no, I wouldn't say I do things without thinking them through. I just get terribly sidetracked along the way.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? Oh, sitting still is just dreadful for me. I’ve never been one to just sit like a bump on a log, but it really does feel like a physical impossibility sometimes. Even when I am absolutely supposed to be completely still, my body just refuses to cooperate. 

Take my church meetings, for example. We have the women's auxiliary meeting every Wednesday morning, and then of course regular service on Sundays. And I try, doctor, I really do try to just sit quietly and listen to Pastor Thomas—he’s been with us for about five years now, a very lovely man, though I will say his sermons can run a little long when he gets on a tangent about the Old Testament. But I’ll be sitting there in the pew, trying my hardest to pay attention, and before I even realize I'm doing it, I am tapping my foot against the floorboards. Just tap, tap, tap, a mile a minute. 

And if I catch myself and force my foot to stop, well, then my hands just take over! I’ll sit there rubbing the edge of my purse. It’s a nice navy blue leather purse I got on sale at Macy's last spring, and I will just run my thumb over the piping on the edge, over and over and over again until the leather is practically worn down. Or I'll be shifting around in the chair, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, adjusting my skirt, scooting forward, leaning back. I just cannot get comfortable. 

I do it so much that the ladies beside me—usually Gladys and Mary, they always sit in the same row as me—they actually start looking over. I can see them out of the corner of my eye, giving me these little sideways glances, and I know they're wondering why I can't just sit in peace. It is so embarrassing! You would think at 66 years old I could sit through an hour of church without wiggling around like a toddler in a high chair, but I just can't. It’s like my muscles get... well, itchy, almost. If I don't move at least some part of my body, I feel like I'm going to jump right out of my own skin. Even at home, if I'm watching a television program, I have to be knitting, or folding laundry, or at the very least bouncing my knee. So yes, sitting still without fidgeting is quite a struggle for me.
Did you experience similar feelings of restlessness and difficulty sitting still when you were a child?

Oh, my, yes. Yes, indeed. It’s certainly not a new thing, not by a long shot. You know, I remember... well, my mother used to keep all of my old report cards in this beautiful cedar hope chest at the foot of her bed. Years later, when I was grown, I was looking through them, and it was just the same story year after year. 

Even way back in grade school, at Lincoln Elementary, my teachers—Mrs. Gable, Mr. Henderson, all of them—they all wrote the exact same things in the little comment boxes. They always noted that I was a bright girl, very capable, you know, but just so terribly careless. That was the word they always used: careless. I was always, always losing my papers. I would sit at the kitchen table and do my spelling words or my arithmetic, I swear to you I did, but by the time the morning bell rang, that paper had just vanished into thin air! I'd be digging through my satchel, turning my desk inside out, and it was just gone.

And the talking... oh, goodness, I was forever getting scolded for talking out of turn. I just had so much to say, and the thoughts would bubble right up and out of my mouth before I even remembered I was supposed to raise my hand. And they were constantly, I mean constantly, having to give me reminders to just stay in my seat. I'd be up wandering over to the pencil sharpener for the third time, or standing up to look out the window to watch the crossing guard, or going over to see what the girl next to me was drawing, and the teacher would have to stop the whole lesson just to tell me to sit back down and finish my work. 

Because I just couldn't seem to get to the end of a worksheet without my legs deciding it was time to go for a stroll! It drove my poor mother half mad, really, because she knew I had the brains for the schoolwork, but I just couldn't stay put long enough to actually get it done and handed in. So, yes, that restless feeling, that absolute impossibility of just sitting still and being quiet... it's been following me around since I was a little girl in pigtails.
Have you noticed any problems with your relationships or daily activities because of these feelings of restlessness and difficulty focusing?

Oh, it’s just awful, doctor. It really is. It’s affecting... well, just about everything, if I’m being completely honest. It has become a terrible burden on the people around me, and that is the hardest part to swallow. 

Just last month, my daughter Susan—she lives about twenty minutes away in the next town over, she’s a dental hygienist—she actually had to come over and completely take over my bills and my paperwork. I had this system, you see, where I kept the important mail in a nice little wicker basket on the kitchen counter, right next to the toaster. But the basket would get full, and I couldn't seem to sit down and focus long enough to sort through it. I'd pull out the water bill, and then I'd get up to find my reading glasses, and then I'd notice the hallway rug was crooked, and by the end of the day, the bill was lost under a stack of old magazines. I ended up with two final notice letters! So Susan finally just said, "Mom, enough is enough," and she took all the paperwork. She set up some sort of automatic payment on the computer for me. It’s humiliating, really, at 66 years old, having your child step in to manage your own household bills because you can't keep your mind on it.

And it’s not just at home with my family. It’s with my friends, too. I mentioned the church auxiliary earlier, and I also belong to a community garden club. We do the floral arrangements for the spring festival every year, and we take it very seriously. Well, I volunteered to organize the tulip bulb order this past fall. I had the catalogs, I had the order forms... but I just kept getting so restless trying to sort through the varieties, or I'd get completely sidetracked and lose the forms altogether. By the time I finally sat down to force myself to do it, the deadline had completely passed. 

Gladys and the other ladies had to completely redo the plans at the very last minute. They had to scramble to buy whatever was left at the local hardware store to cover the responsibilities I had just completely dropped. It was a disaster. 

I am just so terribly embarrassed by it all. I really am. These are groups I care so deeply about, people I’ve known for years and years, and I can just see it in their eyes now... they don't feel they can count on me anymore. They’ll smile and say it’s fine, of course, because they are polite Christian women, but the next time there’s a project, they don't ask me to be in charge. They just give me something simple to do, like bringing the paper napkins. It breaks my heart, doctor, it really does, because I want to be helpful and I want to be involved, but I just end up letting everyone down.
Are there any specific situations or activities where you feel like your restlessness and difficulty focusing are causing the most problems for you?

Well, doctor, if I really sit and think about it, the place it just drives me up the wall the most—aside from the paperwork I mentioned—is when I have to sit down and read something that actually requires my full attention. It’s just... oh, it’s terribly frustrating. 

Take the senior center newsletter, for instance. They mail it out on the first of every month, usually printed on this bright yellow paper so you can't miss it, and it has all the upcoming events, the birthdays, the Tuesday lunch menus, all of that. And I really want to read it, I do! I’ll make myself a nice cup of chamomile tea, sit down at the kitchen table, put on my reading glasses—the ones with the little rhinestones on the corners that Susan bought for me—and I’ll start reading. 

And I start out just fine, I really do. I’ll read the headline, maybe the first paragraph about the upcoming rummage sale or the bingo tournament. But then, after just a few minutes... it’s like my brain just completely unplugs itself. I will suddenly realize that my eyes have been going over the exact same lines, over and over and over again, and I have absolutely no earthly idea what I just read. The words are there, I'm looking right at them, but nothing sticks! 

The exact same thing happens with my choir schedules. I’ve been singing alto in the church choir for, oh, it must be twelve years now, and Director Miller always hands out these very detailed schedules for rehearsals, telling us which hymns we're doing for which Sunday and who has the solos. I can sit down with that choir schedule, and I’ll look at it, and I’m reading the words, but the meaning just floats right out of my head. I’ll read the same sentence five times and then, come Sunday morning, I still have to turn to Gladys and whisper to ask her what page we're supposed to be turning to. It’s just exhausting, doctor, trying so incredibly hard to concentrate on a piece of paper right in front of my face and having absolutely nothing to show for it.
Did your parents or teachers ever suggest that you might have had attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, when you were growing up?

Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. They never used words like that back then. You have to understand, doctor, when I was growing up—this would have been the early sixties—nobody at Lincoln Elementary was talking about things like... well, like what you just said. Attention deficit or whatever it is. It just wasn't something that was on anyone's radar, especially not for a little girl. 

If a boy was bouncing off the walls, they might say he had ants in his pants, but for a girl? Oh, my. If you couldn't sit still, or if you were always losing your spelling papers like I was, they didn't think there was any sort of medical reason for it. They just thought you were a problem child, or that you lacked proper discipline at home. My mother, bless her heart, she would get so terribly flustered after the parent-teacher conferences. She would sit me down at the kitchen table—the one with the yellow formica top, I can still see it—and she would just wring her hands and ask me why I couldn't just behave like the other girls. Why I had to be such a chatterbox, why I was always up and out of my seat. 

But no teacher ever pulled her aside and said they thought I had a condition. Never. Mr. Henderson, Mrs. Gable... they just wrote "careless" and "needs to apply herself" in those little boxes on the report cards, over and over again. They just thought it was a character flaw, you see? A lack of focus or just plain laziness. It makes me a little sad, really, to think back on it now, because I was trying. I swear to you I was trying my very best to be good and to pay attention, but my brain just wouldn't cooperate. 

But no, to answer your question, nobody ever suggested anything like that. Not once. They just thought I was a handful, and that was the end of it. It wasn't until much, much later in life that I even heard those terms used for anyone, let alone for someone like me. I just spent my whole life thinking there was something wrong with my character...
Have you experienced these feelings of restlessness and difficulty focusing consistently throughout your adult life, or have they varied in intensity over the years?

Well, doctor, if I really look back at it... I suppose I’ve always been a little bit, oh, scatterbrained, I guess you could say. Even when Arthur and I first got married, I was always the one misplacing the car keys or forgetting to take the pot roast out of the freezer. But it never... it never ruined my life, you know? It was just one of my little quirks. Arthur, bless his heart, he was a postal worker for thirty-five years, so he was very methodical, very organized. He kept the calendar, he made sure we left on time for church, he just... he anchored me, I suppose. 

But as for it being this severe? This absolute inability to sit still, or the way my brain just turns to mush when I try to read? No, no, it hasn't been like this my whole adult life. The real trouble... the point where it just became entirely unmanageable and started affecting my bills and my friendships like I was telling you... that really started after my husband died. 

It’s been... oh, let me think, it will be exactly a year and ten months ago now. A year and ten months since Arthur passed. 

And at first, you know, everyone tells you it’s just the grief. Susan kept saying, "Oh, Mom, give yourself some grace, it's just the mourning process." "Widow's brain," I think Gladys called it at the garden club. And I believed them! I really did. I thought, well, of course I can't concentrate on sorting the mail, I've just lost my husband of over forty years. But the grief... well, the sharpest part of the crying and the shock, that faded over time, as the Lord intends it to. But this... this terrible restlessness, this feeling like a motor is running inside me and I can't focus on a single earthly thing... it didn't go away with the grief. It just stayed, and it got worse. Without Arthur's routine to keep me in line, everything just completely fell apart. So, no, it hasn't always been this intense. It’s really just been these last twenty-two months without him that it's been causing me such real, undeniable trouble.
Have you experienced these symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing for more than 6 months?

Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor. It’s been quite a bit longer than six months. Like I mentioned, this has all been causing me real, terrible trouble ever since my husband died, which was about a year and ten months ago now. Twenty-two whole months. 

Oh, if it had only been six months, I might still think it was just a passing phase or the initial shock of it all, but it’s been nearly two years of this... this awful feeling. You know, you really count the months when you lose someone, you keep track of every little milestone. I remember when I hit that six-month mark, I thought to myself, "Surely my head will clear by the holidays, surely I'll be able to sit down and read a book again." But then a whole year went by, and the spring came and went, and now we're at a year and ten months, and I'm still just pacing around the house, unable to focus on a single earthly thing. 

So yes, to answer your question, it has definitely been much more than six months. It's been a year and ten months of just absolute chaos, every single day, without Arthur here to keep me grounded.
Have you noticed if these feelings of restlessness and difficulty focusing have been present most days for the past 6 months?

Well, yes, doctor, most days... and really, I'd go so far as to say just about *every* day. It's a daily battle, it truly is. Like I was just telling you, this has been causing me real, undeniable trouble every single day since my husband died, which is about a year and ten months ago now. 

Every morning I wake up, and I think to myself, "Today is the day I'm going to sit down and sort through that mountain of mail on the kitchen table." I make my cup of coffee—just Sanka, usually, because the real caffeinated kind makes my heart flutter too much—and I tell myself I'm going to just sit and focus. But then that terrible restlessness sets in. It's like clockwork. Monday through Sunday, it doesn't matter if it's a regular weekday or the Sabbath. I'll take my coffee cup and before I know it, I'm pacing from the kitchen to the living room, picking up a duster, putting it down, turning on the daytime television, turning it right back off because the noise is too much... it's just exhausting. 

So when you ask if it's been most days for the past six months, I just have to say yes, absolutely, but it's been most days for the past twenty-two months. One year and ten months of waking up every single morning and feeling like a cheap little wind-up toy that someone wound much too tight and just let loose on the linoleum. There hasn't been a single day of peace or focus since Arthur left, really. Not one.
Have you experienced significant problems with restlessness and difficulty focusing for at least 6 months?

Well, doctor, yes, and I think I've been saying that, haven't I? It's been much longer than six months, and it's caused me... well, it's just turned my life completely upside down. It really has. I don't know how else to explain the sheer trouble it's caused me. 

You see, Arthur always handled the bills. He had this little wooden desk in the den, and every Friday evening, he'd sit down with his checkbook and his reading glasses. And when he passed, I thought, well, I can certainly manage to write a check to the electric company. But with this... this awful feeling, this inability to just sit and look at the numbers without my mind racing in a hundred different directions... well, things started slipping through the cracks. It got so bad that Susan—my daughter, Susan—she had to completely step in. She comes over every other week now just to sort through the paperwork and make sure the water isn't going to be shut off. It's humiliating, really. I'm a grown woman, sixty-six years old, and my daughter is treating me like I'm a child who can't manage her own allowance. 

And it's not just the bills, either. It's my social life, the things that used to bring me joy. At the church, I used to be on the committee for the Wednesday night suppers. I was always reliable. But lately... well, these past twenty-two months, I'll volunteer to pick up the paper plates or organize the phone tree, and then the day comes and my mind is just a complete blank, or I'm so restless I've paced a hole in the carpet instead of going to the store. The other ladies have had to redo all my plans or cover for me at the last minute. The same thing happened at the garden club. Gladys had to completely take over the spring bulb sale because I dropped the ball so spectacularly. 

It's just so embarrassing, doctor. I sit in the pews on Sunday, and I can feel them looking at me. I feel like the groups I care so deeply about, the people I've known for years, they just don't feel they can count on me anymore. And they're right! They can't! Because I can't even count on myself to sit still long enough to read a simple recipe, let alone organize a church supper. So, yes, it's been significant problems. Very, very significant.
Have you had these symptoms for at least 6 months, or has it been less than that?

Well, doctor, I... I feel like we might be getting our wires crossed here, or maybe I'm just rambling so much that my point is getting lost in the weeds. But, yes, it has absolutely been at least six months. It hasn't been less than that at all. Like I've been trying to tell you, this... this whole awful situation has been causing me real, genuine trouble ever since my husband died. And that was about a year and ten months ago. 

I know I keep repeating that timeline, but it's just burned into my memory, you know? You don't just forget the day your entire world stops making sense. It was a year and ten months ago, twenty-two months, and I've felt this exact same way every single day since. I even bought one of those large-print calendars down at the pharmacy—the one with the Thomas Kinkade paintings, you know the ones with the little glowing cottages—and I started marking off the weeks, thinking, "Surely by month three I'll be able to concentrate, surely by month six I'll stop pacing the floor." 

But I've gone through an entire calendar and had to buy a new one for this year, and I'm still in the exact same state. I just can't seem to get my feet under me. So, no, it's definitely not less than six months. It's been a year and ten months of just... constant, exhausting trouble.
Have you experienced significant problems with restlessness and difficulty focusing for at least 6 months?

Well, doctor, I... I know you just asked me that, and I know I just answered it, but I really want to make sure you understand just how much this has impacted me. It's not just a little restlessness, it's... well, it's like I said before, it's completely upended my life. The problems are very, very significant. 

I mean, I've had to have my daughter Susan take over my finances. Can you imagine? I raised that girl, I taught her how to balance a checkbook when she was in high school, and now she's the one coming over to my house to make sure I've paid the gas bill. Because if I try to do it, I just... I can't sit still, my mind wanders, and the bills just pile up in that little wire basket on the counter. It's humiliating. 

And then there's the church, and my garden club... I've always been a doer, doctor. I've always been the one people rely on. But these past twenty-two months, since Arthur passed and this... this awful inability to focus started... I've just dropped the ball so many times. I'll volunteer to organize the phone tree for the Wednesday suppers, and then I just... I can't do it. I pace the floor instead. The other ladies have had to step in and redo all my plans, or cover my responsibilities at the very last minute. Gladys taking over the spring bulb sale... that really stung, but I couldn't blame her. I had completely botched the order forms because I couldn't concentrate long enough to read them. 

It's just so embarrassing. I feel like these groups, these people I've known for decades and care about so deeply... they just don't feel they can count on me anymore. And it breaks my heart, because I want to be reliable, I really do, but I just can't seem to get my brain to cooperate. I’ll wash my face, brush my teeth, put on my favorite blue flannel nightgown—the one my daughter bought me for Christmas two years ago, it’s so soft—and I’ll get into bed. target_item.manifestation: This has been causing real trouble since my husband died about 1 year and 10 months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and consistency of my symptoms over my adult life, which corresponds to the duration of my current difficulties (since my husband died 1 year and 10 months ago).

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, if I really look back at it... I suppose I’ve always been a little bit, oh, scatterbrained, I guess you could say. Even when Arthur and I first got married, I was always the one misplacing the car keys or forgetting to take the pot roast out of the freezer. But it never... it never ruined my life, you know? It was just one of my little quirks. Arthur, bless his heart, he was a postal worker for thirty-five years, so he was very methodical, very organized. He kept the calendar, he made sure we left on time for church, he just... he anchored me, I suppose. 

But as for it being this severe? This absolute inability to sit still, or the way my brain just turns to mush when I try to read? No, no, it hasn't been like this my whole adult life. The real trouble... the point where it just became entirely unmanageable and started affecting my bills and my friendships like I was telling you... that really started after my husband died. 

It’s been... oh, let me think, it will be exactly a year and ten months ago now. A year and ten months since Arthur passed. 

And at first, you know, everyone tells you it’s just the grief. Susan kept saying, "Oh, Mom, give yourself some grace, it's just the mourning process." "Widow's brain," I think Gladys called it at the garden club. And I believed them! I really did. I thought, well, of course I can't concentrate on sorting the mail, I've just lost my husband of over forty years. But the grief... well, the sharpest part of the crying and the shock, that faded over time, as the Lord intends it to. But this... this terrible restlessness, this feeling like a motor is running inside me and I can't focus on a single earthly thing... it didn't go away with the grief. It just stayed, and it got worse. Without Arthur's routine to keep me in line, everything just completely fell apart. So, no, it hasn't always been this intense. It’s really just been these last twenty-two months without him that it's been causing me such real, undeniable trouble.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor. It’s been quite a bit longer than six months. Like I mentioned, this has all been causing me real, terrible trouble ever since my husband died, which was about a year and ten months ago now. Twenty-two whole months. 

Oh, if it had only been six months, I might still think it was just a passing phase or the initial shock of it all, but it’s been nearly two years of this... this awful feeling. You know, you really count the months when you lose someone, you keep track of every little milestone. I remember when I hit that six-month mark, I thought to myself, "Surely my head will clear by the holidays, surely I'll be able to sit down and read a book again." But then a whole year went by, and the spring came and went, and now we're at a year and ten months, and I'm still just pacing around the house, unable to focus on a single earthly thing. 

So yes, to answer your question, it has definitely been much more than six months. It's been a year and ten months of just absolute chaos, every single day, without Arthur here to keep me grounded.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the persistence criterion for ADHD
doctor.question: Have you noticed if these feelings of restlessness and difficulty focusing have been present most days for the past 6 months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been causing real trouble since my husband died about 1 year and 10 months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the persistence of the symptoms over the past 6 months, which maps to the duration criteria.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor, most days... and really, I'd go so far as to say just about *every* day. It's a daily battle, it truly is. Like I was just telling you, this has been causing me real, undeniable trouble every single day since my husband died, which is about a year and ten months ago now. 

Every morning I wake up, and I think to myself, "Today is the day I'm going to sit down and sort through that mountain of mail on the kitchen table." I make my cup of coffee—just Sanka, usually, because the real caffeinated kind makes my heart flutter too much—and I tell myself I'm going to just sit and focus. But then that terrible restlessness sets in. It's like clockwork. Monday through Sunday, it doesn't matter if it's a regular weekday or the Sabbath. I'll take my coffee cup and before I know it, I'm pacing from the kitchen to the living room, picking up a duster, putting it down, turning on the daytime television, turning it right back off because the noise is too much... it's just exhausting. 

So when you ask if it's been most days for the past six months, I just have to say yes, absolutely, but it's been most days for the past twenty-two months. One year and ten months of waking up every single morning and feeling like a cheap little wind-up toy that someone wound much too tight and just let loose on the linoleum. There hasn't been a single day of peace or focus since Arthur left, really. Not one.

doctor.question: Have you experienced significant problems with restlessness and difficulty focusing for at least 6 months?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My family has had to step in with bills and paperwork, and people at church and the garden have had to redo plans or cover responsibilities I dropped. I feel embarrassed because groups I care about no longer feel they can count on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about 'significant problems' caused by the symptoms, which relates to the functional impairment experienced by the patient.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, yes, and I think I've been saying that, haven't I? It's been much longer than six months, and it's caused me... well, it's just turned my life completely upside down. It really has. I don't know how else to explain the sheer trouble it's caused me. 

You see, Arthur always handled the bills. He had this little wooden desk in the den, and every Friday evening, he'd sit down with his checkbook and his reading glasses. And when he passed, I thought, well, I can certainly manage to write a check to the electric company. But with this... this awful feeling, this inability to just sit and look at the numbers without my mind racing in a hundred different directions... well, things started slipping through the cracks. It got so bad that Susan—my daughter, Susan—she had to completely step in. She comes over every other week now just to sort through the paperwork and make sure the water isn't going to be shut off. It's humiliating, really. I'm a grown woman, sixty-six years old, and my daughter is treating me like I'm a child who can't manage her own allowance. 

And it's not just the bills, either. It's my social life, the things that used to bring me joy. At the church, I used to be on the committee for the Wednesday night suppers. I was always reliable. But lately... well, these past twenty-two months, I'll volunteer to pick up the paper plates or organize the phone tree, and then the day comes and my mind is just a complete blank, or I'm so restless I've paced a hole in the carpet instead of going to the store. The other ladies have had to redo all my plans or cover for me at the last minute. The same thing happened at the garden club. Gladys had to completely take over the spring bulb sale because I dropped the ball so spectacularly. 

It's just so embarrassing, doctor. I sit in the pews on Sunday, and I can feel them looking at me. I feel like the groups I care so deeply about, the people I've known for years, they just don't feel they can count on me anymore. And they're right! They can't! Because I can't even count on myself to sit still long enough to read a simple recipe, let alone organize a church supper. So, yes, it's been significant problems. Very, very significant.
